steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState from 'react'
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The import statement for React and useState is added.
successCriteria: The code includes an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState from 'react'. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for managing state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement isn't quite complete. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look like the correct import statement. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX. The component should be the default export.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax. Make sure to include a return statement that returns some JSX (like a div).
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the App component here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a functional component named App that returns JSX and is exported as default.
successCriteria: Component named App exists
Component returns JSX
Component is exported as default
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the App component with proper TypeScript typing and default export.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure: 1) The component is named 'App', 2) It returns JSX, and 3) It's exported as default.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a functional component named App that returns JSX and export it as default.

steps.title: Initialize isActive state
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, initialize a boolean state variable called 'isActive' using useState, with an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to use TypeScript's generic syntax for boolean values.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a boolean state variable
const [isVisible, setIsVisible] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: Your component will have a state variable 'isActive' initialized to false, ready to be used for conditional rendering in later steps.
successCriteria: State variable named 'isActive'
Uses useState hook
Initial value is false
TypeScript boolean type annotation
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the isActive state variable. This boolean state will control whether certain UI elements are active or not.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: Did you name the variable 'isActive'? Did you set the initial value to false? Did you use the useState hook?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to use the useState hook to create a boolean state variable called 'isActive' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Define toggle handler function
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, define a function called handleToggle that toggles the isActive state value.
steps.hint: Create a function that uses the setter function from useState to update isActive to the opposite of its current value.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a handleToggle function that correctly toggles the isActive boolean state.
successCriteria: The code should include a function named handleToggle that calls setIsActive with a function that returns the opposite of the current isActive value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a toggle handler function that will update the isActive state when called.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleToggle function properly toggles the boolean value. Use setIsActive with a function that returns !prevState.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleToggle function isn't correctly defined. Remember to create a function that calls setIsActive to toggle the boolean state value.

steps.title: Return a container div
steps.instruction: Inside your App component's return statement, add a <div> element that will serve as the main container for your content.
steps.hint: Place a <div> element inside the return statement's parentheses. This will wrap all the content you'll add later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a <div> element containing the existing <h1> element.
successCriteria: The return statement contains a <div> element
The <div> wraps the existing <h1> element
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a container div that will hold all your content. This provides a proper structure for your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your return statement includes a <div> element that wraps the existing content.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a <div> element containing the <h1>. Check that your return statement has the correct JSX structure.

steps.title: Add a button element
steps.instruction: Inside the container div, add a button element with the text 'Toggle Active'.
steps.hint: Add a <button> element after the existing <h1> element inside the <div>.
steps.expectedOutcome: A button with the text 'Toggle Active' appears inside the container div.
successCriteria: button element
Toggle Active text
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added a button element with the correct text.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but check the text content or placement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element is missing or incorrectly placed.

steps.title: Wire button click to toggle handler
steps.instruction: Add an onClick handler to the button that calls the handleToggle function.
steps.hint: Use the onClick attribute on the button element and set it to the handleToggle function reference.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of wiring a button to a handler
<button onClick={handleToggle}>Toggle</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The button will now respond to clicks and call the handleToggle function.
successCriteria: The button element should have an onClick attribute set to handleToggle.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully connected the button to the toggle handler. Now clicking the button will trigger the state update.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've added the onClick attribute to the button and set it to handleToggle (without parentheses).
steps.feedbackWrong: The button still needs an onClick handler. Add onClick={handleToggle} to the button element.

steps.title: Add button text that reflects state
steps.instruction: Update the button's text content to show 'Active' when isActive is true and 'Inactive' when isActive is false.
steps.hint: Use a ternary expression inside the button's text content to conditionally display different text based on the isActive state.
steps.expectedOutcome: The button text should dynamically change between 'Active' and 'Inactive' when clicked.
successCriteria: The button element should contain a ternary expression that uses isActive to display 'Active' when true and 'Inactive' when false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully made the button text reflect the current state. The ternary expression correctly shows 'Active' or 'Inactive' based on the isActive value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the button text isn't fully dynamic. Make sure you're using a ternary expression with isActive to conditionally display 'Active' or 'Inactive'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button text doesn't reflect the state. You need to replace the static 'Toggle' text with a ternary expression that shows 'Active' when isActive is true and 'Inactive' when false.

steps.title: Create a conditional class string
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a variable named `buttonClass` that builds a class string. The string should be 'active' when `isActive` is true, and an empty string when false.
steps.hint: You can use a ternary operator: `const buttonClass = isActive ? 'active' : '';`
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a conditional class string
const buttonClass = isActive ? 'active' : '';
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a `buttonClass` variable that conditionally returns 'active' or an empty string based on the `isActive` state.
successCriteria: The code must include a variable named `buttonClass` that uses a ternary operator to conditionally assign 'active' or an empty string based on `isActive`.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a conditional class string that will be 'active' when the state is true and empty when false.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using a ternary operator to conditionally assign 'active' or an empty string based on `isActive`.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a variable named `buttonClass` that uses a ternary operator to assign 'active' when `isActive` is true, and an empty string when false.

steps.title: Apply conditional class to button
steps.instruction: Add the className attribute to the existing button element, setting it to the conditional class string you created in the previous step.
steps.hint: The className attribute should be added directly to the button element, similar to how you added the onClick attribute earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The button element should now have a className attribute that dynamically changes between 'active' and 'inactive' based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: The button element has a className attribute
The className attribute value uses the conditional class string (buttonClass)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the className attribute to the button. The button will now have different CSS classes applied based on the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added the className attribute to the button element and set it to the buttonClass variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element still needs the className attribute. Add className={buttonClass} to the button element to apply the conditional class.

steps.title: Add a status display element
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element after the button to display the current status. The paragraph should show 'Status: active' when isActive is true and 'Status: inactive' when isActive is false.
steps.hint:
Insert a

element with text that uses the isActive state variable to conditionally display 'active' or 'inactive'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Add a paragraph that displays status based on state

Status: {isActive ? 'active' : 'inactive'}
steps.expectedOutcome: The UI will now show a paragraph below the button that updates its text based on the isActive state.
successCriteria:
Add a

element after the button
Use isActive state to conditionally display 'active' or 'inactive'
Display text in format 'Status: active' or 'Status: inactive'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a paragraph that displays the current status based on the isActive state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a paragraph, but it doesn't fully meet the requirements. Make sure it displays 'Status: active' when isActive is true and 'Status: inactive' when false.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element is missing or doesn't correctly display the status based on isActive state.

steps.title: Style status display with conditional class
steps.instruction: Apply the same conditional class string to the paragraph element that displays the status.
steps.hint: Add the className attribute to the paragraph element and set it to the buttonClass variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of applying a conditional class to an element

Status: Active
steps.expectedOutcome: The paragraph element will have the same conditional styling as the button, changing its appearance based on the isActive state.
successCriteria: The paragraph element should have a className attribute set to the buttonClass variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've successfully applied the conditional class to the status display, demonstrating how the same conditional logic can be used across multiple elements.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the paragraph element needs to use the buttonClass variable for its className. Make sure you're applying the same conditional class pattern as the button.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraph element should have a className attribute that uses the buttonClass variable to apply conditional styling based on the isActive state.
